q.intro.text: Which points make y greater than x plus one true? Picture all of them on the plane. Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps from single points to the whole picture. Press each step: the plane moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Put points in. Zero, three: three is greater than one, true. Three, one: one is greater than four, false. Negative two, zero point five: zero point five is greater than negative one, true. A point between grid lines counts too. Two, three: three is greater than three is false. The two sides are equal.

e.step1.text: Every point where the sides are equal lies on one line: y equals x plus one, the boundary. The sign is greater than, so equal is not enough: the boundary is drawn dashed, and the point two, three is left out.

e.step2.text: Now one test point off the line. Zero, zero gives zero is greater than one, false. So the solutions are on the other side: above the line. Shade it.

e.step3.text: Why above? At x equals three the line is at y equals four, and y greater than three plus one means y greater than four: everything straight up from the line. The same at every x. So the solutions fill a half-plane: every point above, decimals too, with no end.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does one test point decide the whole side?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. To switch from false to true you would have to pass a point where the sides are equal, and those are all on the line. No crossing, no switch.

e.why.trick.text: It is more than a rule. The sides can only change order where they are equal, and that is only on the line.

e.why.many.text: More tests would all agree. Two points on one side are joined by a path that never meets the line, so the answer cannot change.

t.intro.text: Your turn: graph three x minus two y is greater than or equal to six. The x-intercept is done for you: y equals zero gives three x equals six, so the point two, zero.

t.y.text: Now the y-intercept: put x equal to zero. What is y?

t.y.ok.text: Yes: negative two y equals six, so y equals negative three. The boundary runs through two, zero and zero, negative three.

t.y.swap.text: Two is the x-intercept. For the y-intercept, x is zero: negative two y equals six.

t.y.sign.text: Mind the sign: negative two y equals six, and six divided by negative two is negative three.

t.y.no.text: Put x equal to zero: negative two y equals six. Divide by negative two.

t.st.text: Is the boundary solid or dashed?

t.st.ok.text: Yes: greater than or equal lets equal in, so the points on the line are solutions: solid.

t.st.no.text: Greater than or equal means greater than, or equal. On the line the two sides are equal, and that counts: solid.

t.side.text: Test zero, zero: three times zero minus two times zero is zero, and zero is greater than or equal to six is false. Which side do you shade?

t.side.ok.text: Yes: zero, zero is above the line and fails, so shade below. Check four, zero: twelve is greater than or equal to six. It checks. The sign said above, the test point said below: with negative two y, the sign alone does not tell.

t.side.above.text: Greater than or equal only means above when y is alone with a plus sign. Here it is negative two y. Trust the test point: zero, zero is above and false.

t.side.origin.text: Zero, zero made it false. A false test point means: shade the other side.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked every point above, not the line, and you were right. Now you know why: the boundary is where the sides are equal, and one test point picks the side.

q.cb.line.text: At the start you picked only the points on the line. Those are the points where the sides are equal. Greater than asks for a whole side of the plane.

q.cb.incl.text: At the start you picked above, and the line too. The line is where y equals x plus one exactly, and greater than leaves equal out: dashed.

q.cb.none.text: Boundary first, dashed or solid from the sign, then one test point picks the side.

p.intro.text: Jordan graphs the system y is greater than or equal to two x plus one, and y is less than or equal to two x minus three, and shades the strip between the lines. Two inequalities always make a region. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Zero, negative one sits in the strip of Jordan, but negative one is greater than or equal to one is false. A shaded point that fails is evidence the strip is wrong.

p.c2.text: Right. The first one shades above the upper line, the second below the lower line: they point away from each other.

p.c3.text: Right. Both at once would need two x plus one to be at most y, and y at most two x minus three. So one would be at most negative three: false for every x.

p.no.always.text: That is the claim of Jordan, not a reason. Parallel boundaries can face away from each other, and then nothing is shared.

p.no.one.text: A solution of a system must make every inequality true at the same point.

p.no.example.text: One failing point does not prove that every point fails. That needs a reason that covers all x.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: a counterexample in the strip, the two half-planes facing away, and an argument for every x. The system has no solution, and nothing should be shaded.
